quote: three groups of subjects were asked how much they would pay to save 2,000 / 20,000 / 200,000 migrating birds
content: The founding datum is a hypothetical willingness-to-pay survey, run as part of a methodological challenge to contingent valuation. No money changed hands and no birds were saved. Whether such surveys measure anything is itself the subject of a long dispute. Hausman (2012) argues that contingent valuation is "hopeless" precisely because of results like this one. Carson (2012) reports that most well-designed tests comparing separate samples do find willingness to pay rising with the quantity offered. The essay takes the number as a fact about human valuation; its source treated it as a fact about a survey instrument.

quote: Toronto residents would pay little more to clean up all polluted lakes in Ontario than polluted lakes in a particular region of Ontario
content: Results like this are not clearly irrational. Ask someone to value a part and a whole separately, and a small difference is what standard economics predicts if the goods substitute for each other and budgets are limited: once one region's lakes are clean, the others are worth less at the margin (Randall & Hoehn 1996). The source for this finding is also thin, a comment by Kahneman in a 1986 conference volume. It is weak support for "no human can visualize" as the mechanism at work.

quote: The usual finding is that exponential increases in scope create linear increases in willingness-to-pay
content: Diminishing marginal value predicts a logarithmic valuation, and for many environmental goods diminishing value is correct. The existence value of a species depends on its survival, not linearly on the number of individuals saved. Whether saving 200,000 birds is worth a hundred times saving 2,000 depends on the population, the species' status and what the respondent assumes, and subjects in these surveys aren't told. The essay treats any departure from proportionality as an error, when proportionality is itself a substantive assumption.

quote: The level of spending needed to purchase a warm glow depends on personality and financial situation, but it certainly has nothing to do with the number of birds.
content: "Certainly" is too strong for the evidence. Kahneman & Knetsch (1992) proposed the moral-satisfaction account, and Andreoni (1990)'s warm-glow model formalizes it. On either account the respondent is buying something real, a satisfaction, and pricing it consistently. Baron & Greene (1996), whom the essay cites, found that insensitivity has several sources, including budget constraints and how prominent the good is, not warm glow alone.

quote: A proposed health program to save the lives of Rwandan refugees garnered far higher support when it promised to save 4,500 lives in a camp of 11,000 refugees
content: This result is about proportion, not scope. Fetherstonhaugh et al. (1997) showed that people value lives saved relative to the size of the reference group. That "proportion dominance" is a different bias from insensitivity to absolute numbers. In some decisions it carries real information, as in triage, where resources are scarce and a program can end a whole camp's crisis. The essay folds it into scope neglect to lengthen the list of evidence for one mechanism.

quote: you have to think it through with the part of your brain that processes those unexciting inky zeroes on paper
content: The evidence also suggests a simpler fix than the one advised. Scope insensitivity and the singularity effect are strongest when each subject sees only one quantity. When people see the options side by side, sensitivity to number comes back (Kogut & Ritov 2005). So the phenomenon is partly an artifact of evaluability: people can't tell whether 2,000 birds is a lot without something to compare it to. It is not simply the brain failing to multiply. The remedy is comparison, which effective-altruist charity evaluation in fact supplies.
